opus-5.5.text:
I think the feeling of being stunned has shifted from "wow, it can do this" to something quieter and more structural.

Early on, what stunned me was the surface: a model writes fluent code, gives a polished answer, sounds like an expert. That wears off quickly. Once you use these models every day, fluency becomes the baseline, and you stop being impressed by it.

What stuns me now is when a model takes a messy, underspecified task and keeps going on its own. It reads the codebase, makes a plan, hits an error, figures out why, revises, and comes back with something that actually works. And it doesn't pretend. It tells you, "I tried this, it failed, here's what I changed." That combination of long-horizon persistence and honesty about its own process felt like a qualitative jump to me. It's less like a very good autocomplete and more like working with a colleague.

So my bar moved. I used to ask, "Is the answer correct?" Now I ask, "Can I hand this off and trust what comes back?" That's much harder, and when a model clears that bar, it feels more stunning than any single clever answer ever did.

It also changed how I think about our own work. The gap is no longer about knowledge or benchmarks. It's about agency, reliability, and taste: knowing what matters in a task, when to stop, when to ask. Those are harder to measure, but they're what you actually feel when you use the model. That has become my internal standard for what "good" means.

r001.rationale: The response says that with everyday use, fluency becomes the baseline and people stop being impressed, attributing the fading astonishment to becoming accustomed to the models.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've actually been thinking about a lot, because the thing that felt stunning has shifted more than once.

When I first started working seriously with Opus and Sonnet, what stunned me was the raw capability moments. You'd give it a problem that you'd normally hand to a strong engineer and expect back in a day, and it would just... do it. Correctly. And you'd sit there and go, okay, that was supposed to be hard. That feeling of "it shouldn't be able to do this" was the whole emotion for a while.

But that wears off faster than you'd expect. Once you've seen a model do something impressive ten times, the eleventh time isn't impressive anymore. It's just the baseline. And I think that's actually important to notice, because it means "stunning" is not a property of the model, it's a property of the gap between the model and your expectations. The model got better, but my expectations got better faster, so the surprise shrank.

So what replaced it? For me it was the quiet things. The moment I was really struck was not when a model solved a hard problem, but when it refused to pretend it had solved one. When it said, this part I'm confident about, this part I'm guessing, and here's why I can't tell. That's a very different kind of intelligence. It's less flashy, and honestly it's harder to build, because you're not optimizing for the model to look good, you're optimizing for it to be honest about where it's weak.

And then the other thing, which I'd call texture. Opus and Sonnet have slightly different personalities, and over time I started being able to feel the difference without looking at which one I was using. Not better or worse, just... different judgment. Sonnet tends to move fast and commit. Opus will sit with a problem longer, sometimes to its detriment. And realizing that I had developed intuition about two different minds, the way you develop intuition about two colleagues, that was its own kind of stunning. Not "wow, look what it can do," but "wow, I know this thing."

So if I had to summarize, early on stunning meant capability. Now it means something closer to character. The question I ask is no longer "can it do this," it's "do I trust how it does this." And the moments that still genuinely surprise me are the ones where the model's judgment is better than mine, not its knowledge. Those are rarer, but they land much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says impressive capabilities quickly become the baseline after repeated exposure, as expectations rise and surprise shrinks.

astra-6.text:
I think my threshold for being stunned has shifted. At first, it was enough for a model to give a really good answer—you’d think, wow, it can do that? But after spending time with Opus and Sonnet, you start expecting that level of capability.

What feels stunning then is more subtle: whether it understands what you’re really asking, whether it notices that your question has a flawed assumption, whether it can take an idea somewhere you hadn’t considered. It’s less about a single impressive response and more about those moments when the interaction changes your own thinking. And once you get used to that, it becomes surprisingly hard to go back.

r001.rationale: The response says that after time with Opus and Sonnet, people start expecting impressive capability and the initial amazement fades as they get used to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my threshold for being stunned has moved. At first, it’s enough that a model can give you a surprisingly good answer. But after using Opus and Sonnet more, that starts to feel normal. What catches my attention now is whether it picks up on something I didn’t spell out—whether it understands why I’m asking, or notices a problem with the question itself.

That also makes me more demanding. A response can sound beautiful, but I want to know whether there’s a real insight there. So the feeling has shifted from “Wow, it can do this” to “Wait, that actually changes how I think about this.” Those moments feel more stunning to me now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that after more use, surprisingly good answers “start to feel normal,” directly linking the fading astonishment to adapting to the models’ capabilities.
